title: Adding Lexical Scope Chains and Closures to Our Scheme Interpreter
description: Upgrade a single-dictionary Scheme evaluator with Env parent links and Closure objects so lambda functions capture their definition environment.

steps.description: `tokenize` and `read` parse S-expressions into nested Python lists, integers, and symbol strings, and `PRIMITIVES` maps built-in operator names to Python lambdas.

`Env` holds `self.table = dict(zip(names, values))` and `self.parent = parent`. `Closure` bundles `self.params`, `self.body`, and `self.env` (the `Env` active when the `lambda` was evaluated). Line 52 seeds `global_env` with `PRIMITIVES`.

`evaluate(x, env)` takes the current `env` on every recursive call. Evaluating `lambda` on line 68 returns `Closure(x[1], x[2], env)`, and calling a `Closure` on lines 70-73 builds `call_env = Env(function.params, args, function.env)` and evaluates `function.body` inside `call_env`.

Look at the third argument to `Env(...)` on line 72: `call_env`'s parent is `function.env` (where the closure was defined on line 68), not `env` (where the call happened). That single choice implements static (lexical) scoping.
Lines 85-95 run three tests: parameter shadowing (`(shadow 5)` followed by `x`), a curried closure (`(define add3 (adder 3))` followed by `(add3 4)`), and recursive `fact` (`(fact 5)`).

steps.question: On lines 90-92, `(adder 3)` returns the inner `(lambda (b) (+ a b))` as `add3`, and then `(add3 4)` runs in `global_env`. Which environment is the parent of `call_env` during `(add3 4)`, and what does `(+ a b)` return?
steps.answer: When `(adder 3)` ran, it created an `Env` binding `a = 3` and stored that `Env` as `add3.env`. Calling `(add3 4)` links `call_env` (`b = 4`) to `add3.env` (`a = 3`), so `(+ a b)` returns `7`.

steps.description: At trace step 23 while initializing `global_env`, line 32 populates `self.table` with the built-in primitive procedures from `PRIMITIVES`.
